title: Ambulances hamstrung; Paramedic testifies he broke rules to try to help Robert Carpenter
article: Residents of Amherstburg and rural areas across the province receive inferior ambulance service compared to city dwellers, a coroner's inquest into the shooting death of Robert Scott Carpenter heard Friday.

The inquest was told paramedics who volunteer with Amherstburg's ambulance service are prohibited from administering a range of emergency drugs even if they're qualified to do so. They are only permitted to use five "symptom-relief" drugs.
Tim Branch, the ALS paramedic dispatched to Carpenter's McCurdy Drive home at 7:20 a.m. last Oct. 30, testified he arrived at 7:30 a.m. to find Carpenter lying on the front lawn without vital signs.

He said two Amherstburg police officers trained as paramedics -- Const. Matthew Capel-Cure and Const. Viktor Burany -- were tending to Carpenter's injuries. He described it as a "load and go" situation, his ambulance departing for Hotel-Dieu Grace Hospital after seven minutes.
Branch is qualified to administer a range of emergency drugs and, despite restrictions when working for Amherstburg's service, attempted to resuscitate Carpenter with lidocaine.
The ambulance was not given an escort by Amherstburg police but eventually received one from LaSalle police. Carpenter arrived at hospital at 8:01 a.m., still without vital signs.

Dr. Paul Bradford testified eight units of O-negative blood were ordered. There wasn't much bleeding as Carpenter had no blood pressure. Bradford testified he has never successfully resuscitated a patient who had been without vital signs for more than 20 minutes.

Bradford examined Capel-Cure at the hospital and testified the officer was "distraught" and had a superficial three-cm "linear cut" on his left shoulder. He said it looked like a knife wound but could have been caused by shards of broken glass.

Bradford and Dr. Raymond Forse, who performed emergency surgery on Carpenter, said they never saw the bullet lodged in Carpenter's leg. They said it would have been impossible for someone to remove the fatal bullet and replace it with another.

Carpenter's common-law widow, Lisa Stewart, maintains her husband was shot by Sgt. Bart DiPasquale with a brass-coloured gun and not by Const. Shawn McCurdy with his service revolver. Confronted with forensic evidence contradicting her version of events, Stewart said she saw a police officer in the operating room where her husband died.
Wayne Russelo, the paramedic who tended to DiPasquale and McCurdy at the scene, said the officers were "pale and drawn" after the shooting.
He said DiPasquale had cuts on his forehead, a split lip and dried blood on his face, hands and upper arms. He lifted DiPasquale's shirt to find a small puncture wound.
